issues.legal_issue: A legal question based on the pleadings and evidence may be raised for the first time in a second appeal, but a party cannot claim prejudice from a plea that was rejected and not appealed.
material_facts: In the second appeal, the opposing side raised a new contention about how the firm’s assets should be dealt with on dissolution.
The High Court rejected that contention, and the party that raised it did not appeal against that rejection.
issues.conclusion: The objection to the High Court considering the new contention failed; the contention had been rejected, and no appeal had been brought against that finding. A legal question grounded in the pleadings and evidence may be raised for the first time in a second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: A question of law arising from the pleadings and evidence may be raised for the first time before the High Court. Unlike Hardayal Gir v. Sohna Ram, where a new plea was accepted and prejudiced the opposing party, the plea here was rejected. Under Article 136, as discussed in Santakumari v. Lakshmi Amma Janaki Amma and Chandra Singh v. State of Rajasthan, the Court does not interfere absent grave injustice.

predicates.second_appeal_proceeding: The challenged decision was made in a proceeding that was a second appeal.
predicates.record_based_legal_question: A party raised a legal question grounded in the pleadings and evidence already on the record.
predicates.plea_rejected_without_appeal: The court rejected the newly raised contention, and the party that raised it did not appeal that rejection.

issues.definition: When a legal question in a second appeal rests on the existing record and the contention was rejected without an appeal against that rejection, the opposing party has no material grievance from the court considering it.

issues.legal_issue: A partnership consisting of two partners is dissolved by the death of either partner even if the partnership agreement provides that death will not dissolve the firm, where the remaining partner cannot continue the same partnership without the other partner’s agreement.
material_facts: The firm had only two partners.
The deed stated that the firm would continue for a fixed term and that a partner’s death would not dissolve it.
One partner died, and that partner’s legal representatives were not willing to continue the firm or enter into a new partnership.
issues.conclusion: The firm stood dissolved on the death of one of its two partners notwithstanding the deed’s contrary clause.
issues.legal_principle: Section 42(c) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, makes dissolution on a partner’s death subject to the partners’ contract, but a two-partner firm cannot continue as the same partnership after one partner dies. Under Section 4, partnership is a contractual relationship, not a heritable status; the deceased partner’s legal representatives cannot be compelled to form a new partnership. The Court relied on Smt. S. Parvathammal v. CIT.

rule.if: partnership_dissolution_proceeding and two_partner_firm and partner_died and surviving_partner_cannot_continue_without_new_agreement

predicates.partnership_dissolution_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a partnership firm has been dissolved.
predicates.two_partner_firm: The firm consisted of two partners.
predicates.partner_died: One of the partners died while the firm was in existence.
predicates.surviving_partner_cannot_continue_withou: Continuing the partnership after the death would require the other partner or the deceased partner’s representatives to enter into a new agreement, and they did not agree to do so.

issues.definition: In a dissolution proceeding, when a two-partner firm loses a partner by death and continuation requires a new agreement that is not made, the firm is dissolved on that partner’s death.

issues.legal_issue: On dissolution, property owned by the partners individually does not become partnership property merely because it was used for the business, and the partners may recover their respective property, with compensation for structures that cannot be removed from another partner’s land.
material_facts: One partner provided land for use in the cinema business, while the other partner funded construction and provided business equipment and other movables.
The Court found that the parties had not intended the land and the relevant building assets to become property of the firm.
The structures were embedded in the land and could not be removed without damage; the accounts were also to be settled.
issues.conclusion: The land was to remain in the landowner’s possession, the other partner could remove the movables, and the landowner was to pay the assessed value of structures that could not be removed, after adjustment for any amount due on the partnership accounts.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, makes the definition of partnership property subject to the partners’ agreement. Property belonging to a partner does not become partnership property merely through its use in the business; an express or implied agreement to treat it as partnership property is required. The Court relied on Arjun Kanoji Tankar v. Santaram Kanoji Tankar and Arm Group Enterprises Ltd. v. Waldorf Restaurant, and considered the terms of the partnership deed, including its provision for the property at the end of the term.

rule.if: dissolved_partnership_proceeding and partner_owned_land_used_for_business and other_partner_funded_construction_and_movables and no_agreement_to_treat_assets_as_firm_property and structures_embedded_and_not_removable_without_damage

predicates.dissolved_partnership_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the distribution of property after a partnership has dissolved.
predicates.partner_owned_land_used_for_business: A partner owned land that was used for the partnership business.
predicates.other_partner_funded_construction_and_mo: The other partner funded construction on the land and provided movable business assets.
predicates.no_agreement_to_treat_assets_as_firm_pro: The partners did not expressly or impliedly agree to treat the relevant land and assets as property of the firm.
predicates.structures_embedded_and_not_removable_wi: Structures on the land were embedded in it and could not be removed without damage.

issues.definition: After dissolution, where a partner’s land was used for the business, the other partner funded construction and movables, the assets were not agreed to be firm property, and structures cannot be removed safely, the land and removable assets go to their respective owners and compensation is paid for the irremovable structures.
